# Task 1



In this task we will analyse data consisting of monthly totals of international airline passengers in years 1949 to 1960.
We will try to fit various SARIMA models and choose the best.
Then we will make numbers of passengers forecasts for each month until the end of 2026 using our model.



```{r}
SPKW <- read.csv("SPKW.csv")
data <- ts(SPKW$passengers, start = c(2010, 1), frequency = 12)

plot.ts(data, main = 'Number of passengers over time', col = 'navyblue', xlab = 'year', ylab = '');abline(h=mean(data), col = 'darkred', lty = 2)
```
```{r stacionarity tests}
adf.test(data)
kpss.test(data)
```


```{r}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
acf(na.omit(data), lag.max = 36, main = 'data')
pacf(na.omit(data), lag.max = 36, main = '')
```
```{r}
sum(is.na(data))
```

```{r}
data_diff_12<-diff(data,lag=12)

plot.ts(data_diff_12, main = 'lag-12 difference', col = 'navyblue', xlab = 'year', ylab = '');abline(h=mean(data_diff_12), col = 'darkred', lty = 2)
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
acf(na.omit(data_diff_12), lag.max = 36, main = 'lag-12 difference')
pacf(na.omit(data_diff_12), lag.max = 36, main = '')
```
By applying a seasonal difference (lag-12), we have removed the seasonality, which sets our parameter D = 1. 
However, the sample PACF shows a strong significant spike at the first lag (around 0.8), and the ACF decays very slowly.
This clearly suggests that the series is still highly autocorrelated and requires further first-order differencing (d = 1).

```{r}
adf.test(na.omit(data_diff_12))
kpss.test(na.omit(data_diff_12))
lag.plot(na.omit(data_diff_12), lags = 1, do.lines = FALSE, 
         main = "Wykres opóźnień (Lag-1) dla data_diff_12", 
         col = "navyblue", pch = 16)
```

Although formal stationarity tests (ADF and KPSS) suggest that seasonal differencing alone might be sufficient, the lag plot reveals a strong, positive linear relationship between $Y_t$ and $Y_{t-1}$. This confirms the high autocorrelation (approx. 0.8) previously seen in the PACF plot. To ensure the stability of our SARIMA model and address this near-non-stationarity, we decided to apply an additional first-order difference ($d = 1$).

```{r}
data_diff_12_1<-diff(data_diff_12,lag=1)

plot.ts(data_diff_12_1, main = 'lag-12 then lag-1 difference', col = 'navyblue', xlab = 'year', ylab = '');abline(h=mean(data_diff_12_1), col = 'darkred', lty = 2)
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
acf(na.omit(data_diff_12_1), lag.max = 36, main = 'lag-12 than lag-1 difference')
pacf(na.omit(data_diff_12_1), lag.max = 36, main = '')
```
```{r}
lag.plot(na.omit(data_diff_12_1), lags = 1, do.lines = FALSE, 
         main = "Wykres opóźnień (Lag-1) dla data_diff_12", 
         col = "navyblue", pch = 16)
```


```{r}
adf.test(na.omit(data_diff_12_1))
kpss.test(na.omit(data_diff_12_1))
```
The lag plot for the twice-differenced data now shows a random scatter of points, indicating that the correlation between consecutive observations is close to zero. Both the ADF and KPSS tests confirm that the series data_diff_12_1 is strictly stationary.

The visual analysis of the fully differenced series supports the parameters $d = 1$ and $D = 1$. For the seasonal component, both the ACF and PACF plots cut off at lag $1s$, suggesting $P=0, Q=1$ or $P=1, Q=0$. For the non-seasonal component, the ACF cuts off at lag 1 and the PACF either cuts off at lag 1 or tails off slowly, pointing towards $p=0, q=1$ or $p=1, q=1$ as potential candidates.

```{r}
model_1 <- sarima(data, 0,1,1,0,1,1,12)
model_2 <- sarima(data, 0,1,1,1,1,0,12)
model_3 <- sarima(data, 0,1,1,1,1,1,12)
model_4 <- sarima(data, 1,1,1,0,1,1,12)
model_5 <- sarima(data, 1,1,1,1,1,0,12)
model_6 <- sarima(data, 1,1,1,1,1,1,12)
auto.arima(data)
model_auto <- sarima(data, 0,1,1)
```

After considering AIC of each model, checking whether coefficients are significant and  residuals satisfy our assumptions, we concluded that the first model fits our data best.


```{r}
pred_1 <- sarima.for(data, n.ahead = 12,0,1,1,0,1,1,12)
```


















# Task 2


The dataset **Sales of Shampoo over a Three Year Period** contains monthly shampoo sales observations for three consecutive years. It has 36 observations in total: one month identifier and one numerical sales value for each month. The data is available on Kaggle: <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/djokester/sales-of-shampoo-over-a-three-year-period>.


The goal of this project is to analyze the shampoo sales time series and transform it into a stationary series that can be treated as noise. First, the original data is plotted and checked for trend and seasonality. Then, transformations such as Box-Cox transformation, first differencing and seasonal differencing are applied. Finally, if the transformed series is stationary, an ARMA(p, q) model is selected for the stationary noise.





## Load data


```{r}
shampoo = read.csv("sales-of-shampoo-over-a-three-ye.csv")
shampoo_ts = ts(na.omit(shampoo[2]), start = c(1, 1), frequency = 12)
head(shampoo,10)
```



## Function for adding month names to the plot

```{r}
month_names = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
                "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")

plot_monthly_ts = function(x, main = NULL, ylab = NULL) {
  plot(x, xaxt = "n", xlab = "Miesiąc", ylab = ylab, main = main)
  axis(1,at = time(x),labels = month_names[cycle(x)],las = 2)
}
```

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
plot_monthly_ts(shampoo_ts, main = "Sales of shampoo", ylab = "Sales")
```

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
acf(shampoo_ts, lag.max = 40)
pacf(shampoo_ts, lag.max=40)
```

The plot of the series shows a clear upward trend with maybe some seasonality, that is confirmed by the acf plot. This is clearly not white noise type of series.


To transform the series into white noise, first we can try Box-Cox transformation.



```{r}
lambda = BoxCox.lambda(shampoo_ts)

print(paste('Lambda used in BoxCox transformation is equal to:',round(lambda,4)))


bc_sh = BoxCox(shampoo_ts, lambda = lambda)
```
```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
par(mfrow = c(2,1))
plot_monthly_ts(shampoo_ts, main = "Shampoo sales before Box-Cox", ylab = "Sales before Box-Cox")
plot_monthly_ts(bc_sh, main = "Box-Cox transformed shampoo sales", ylab = "Sales after Box-Cox")

```

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
acf(bc_sh, lag.max = 40)
pacf(bc_sh, lag.max = 40)
```

It appears that Box-Cox transformation had no bigger effect on the data,which was expected since from the plot of the original series -  we cannot see variance increasing over time.


# Trend/seasonality removal
Periodogram




```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
n = length(bc_sh)
Per= Mod(fft(bc_sh-mean(bc_sh)))^2/n  # 
Freq = (1:n -1)/n
plot(Freq[1:n], Per[1:n], type='h', lwd=2, ylab="Periodogram",
     xlab="Frequency")    
```

```{r}
nn=n/2
y = cbind(1:nn, Freq[1:nn], 1/Freq[1:nn],Per[1:nn]); y[order(y[,4],decreasing = TRUE),] # another way to find the  peaks is to order by Per
```

We see some seasonality with 3 years cycle, 1.5 year and 1 year.




We will try to remove trend - first using lag 1


```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
shampoo_diff = diff(bc_sh, lag=1)
plot_monthly_ts(shampoo_diff, main = "Shampoo sales lag 1", ylab = "Sales")

```

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
acf(shampoo_diff,lag.max = 40)
pacf(shampoo_diff,lag.max = 40)

```


Now we remove yearly cycle

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
shampoo_diff_12 = diff(shampoo_diff, lag =12)
plot_monthly_ts(shampoo_diff_12, main = "Shampoo sales lag 12", ylab = "Sales")

```



```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
acf(shampoo_diff_12,lag.max = 40)
pacf(shampoo_diff_12,lag.max = 40)
```

ADF Test
```{r}
adf.test(shampoo_diff_12)

```
The ADF test suggest that the data is stationary, so we will try to fit ARMA models


# ARMA
We will try to fit arma model by hand and using auto.arima, then we will compare it to the models we created manually



```{r}

arma_model_auto <- auto.arima(
  shampoo_diff_12,
  d = 0,
  D = 0,
  seasonal = FALSE,
  stationary = TRUE,
  stepwise = FALSE,
  approximation = FALSE
)

arma_model_auto
```





We do not see clear cut off on ACF and PACF - both of them  so we will try multiple arma models.

```{r}
arma_model_1_1 <- arima(shampoo_diff_12,order = c(1,0,1))
arma_model_1_2 <- arima(shampoo_diff_12,order = c(1,0,2))
arma_model_1_3 <- arima(shampoo_diff_12,order = c(1,0,3))


arma_model_2_1 <- arima(shampoo_diff_12,order = c(2,0,1))
#arma_model_3_1 <- arima(shampoo_diff_12,order = c(3,0,1)) skip - auto arima already choose this model


arma_model_2_2 <- arima(shampoo_diff_12,order = c(2,0,2))
arma_model_3_3 <- arima(shampoo_diff_12,order = c(3,0,3))


```




# Testing the models

AIC
```{r}
AIC_res <- AIC(arma_model_auto, arma_model_1_1, arma_model_1_2, arma_model_1_3,arma_model_2_1,arma_model_2_2,arma_model_3_3)
AIC_res[order(AIC_res$AIC), ]
```

BIC
```{r}
BIC_res <- BIC(arma_model_auto, arma_model_1_1, arma_model_1_2, arma_model_1_3,arma_model_2_1,arma_model_2_2,arma_model_3_3)
BIC_res[order(BIC_res$BIC), ]
```

Comparing 3 best

```{r}
arma_model_1_1
```

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
checkresiduals(arma_model_1_1)
```


```{r}
arma_model_auto
```

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
checkresiduals(arma_model_auto)
```

```{r}
arma_model_3_3
```

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=7}
checkresiduals(arma_model_3_3)
```




Each of the models seems to fit pretty well:

 - All three of the residual plots seem to be white noise
 - ACF plots are situated between blue borders
 - Histograms of residuals seem to be bell shaped
 - Ljung-Box test pass with p value larger than 0.05, although model ARMA(3,0,3) had the lowest p value (0,09) - much smaller than for ARMA(3,0,1) - (0.67) 


# Forecast

```{r,fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
future_1_1<-forecast(arma_model_1_1,h=12,level=95 )
future_auto_3_1<-forecast(arma_model_auto,h=12,level=95 )
future_3_3<-forecast(arma_model_3_3,h=12,level=95 )


par(mfrow = c(3,1))


plot(future_1_1)
plot(future_auto_3_1)
plot(future_3_3)
```



Model ARMA(3,0,1) seems to be the best fit for our dataset.
